newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish companies in wave of share redemptions.
newsitem.headline: Swedish companies in wave of share redemptions.

text.p: While a Swedish company law committee on Wednesday said it would propose that corporations be allowed to buy back their own shares, companies tired of waiting have already resorted to share redemption.

"Share redemption is a new trend," said Hakan Telander, analyst at Handelsbanken. "More companies are likely to use the opportunity to reduce their cash pile, among them (steel group) SSAB and (holding company) Investor."

With share buybacks companies buy back their own shares and then at a later stage have the option to either redeem them or sell them back to the stock market, while share redemption means shares are cancelled.

Overcapitalised Swedish companies have long been promoting the idea of share buy backs, which are allowed in several other countries but not in Sweden, and the company law committee has been expected to propose a change.

"The committee will propose that corporations will be allowed to buy back their own shares and that this rule will be valid as of January 1, 1999," Rolf Skog, secretary to the committee, told Reuters on Wednesday.
But recently several companies have chosen share redemption, among them engineer Sandvik.
"Sandvik has, for some time, awaited legislation allowing share buy backs," the company said in connection with releasing 1996 earnings this week.

"Since there is still uncertainty regarding this legislation, the board has decided to investigate alternative measures to improve capital structure, such as reduction of the share capital through a redemption of shares."
Other companies planning share redemptions are automotive group Volvo, bank Nordbanken, insurer Trygg-Hansa, real estate group Hufvudstaden as well as holding companies Ratos and Custos.
In total, these companies and Sandvik will redeem shares roughly worth 20 billion crowns.
"There is a new trend in the Swedish business sector not to sit on such a large cash pile as previously," Lars Glemstedt, analyst at Aros Securities, told Reuters.
"Earlier many companies seem to have felt the need to have lots of cash in the case they found an interesting acquisition opportunity or needed the money for other things."
Analysts favour less excessive cash as it enables companies to have a higher return on equity, boosting share prices.
"The number of shares on the market falls and then you can upgrade the company," Telander said.

"In addition, with share redemption or share buy back the capital flow to the market remains strong," he said, referring to the fact that shareholders who sell their shares to the company are likely to buy other shares.
Share buy back would be somewhat more beneficial to companies than share redemption, analysts said.
"(Share buyback) would be positive," Telander said. "They already buy back shares in Europe and, mainly, in the U.S."
"It means companies can hold a stake in themselves, which in turn could reduce the takeover risk."
